analysis.one_liner: Standardizes prior authorization rules for the most common high-cost services in Medicare Advantage plans.
analysis.headline: The Prior Authorization Relief Act was introduced in the Senate in February 2026 and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has had no further action and only one Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to audit which medical services and drugs in Medicare Advantage have the highest reimbursements, the strongest clinical evidence, and the most burdensome approval steps, then write one standard set of prior authorization rules for those services that every Medicare Advantage plan must follow. Providers in certain risk-sharing arrangements, such as accountable care organizations, would be exempt from the standardized rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees who face delays or denials when their plan requires advance approval for care, and the doctors and hospitals that spend staff time on repetitive approval paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage patients facing care delays

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to audit prior authorization rules for Medicare Advantage services and drugs, identifying those in the top 10 percent of reimbursements that have sufficient clinical evidence for a standard policy and require an excessive number of steps [S2].

Requires a final rule by May 1, 2028 standardizing prior authorization requirements, including forms, for those identified services across all Medicare Advantage plans, so patients get the same rules no matter which plan they are in [S2].

Exempts services and drugs furnished by providers participating in two-sided risk models, such as accountable care organizations, from the standardized requirements, reducing approval friction in those arrangements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, which would lose some control over utilization management for high-cost services and could shift costs or restrict benefits in other ways; federal taxpayers could see higher Medicare spending if fewer denials mean more care is delivered.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and Medicare spending

drawbacks.text: The reform is narrow: it standardizes rules only for services in the top 10 percent of reimbursements that meet specific audit criteria, so most items subject to prior authorization would be untouched [S2].

The exemption for two-sided risk models lets some providers escape the standardized rules entirely, and insurers can even request that the exemption not apply, which could leave patients facing a patchwork of rules depending on who treats them [S2].

Insurers argue prior authorization controls waste and costs; curbing it could raise Medicare Advantage utilization and, in turn, federal spending or plan premiums, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief for patients and doctors is real but modest, since it covers only the most burdensome and best-documented prior authorization cases. The risk-sharing exemption creates uneven rules, and any increase in Medicare spending from reduced denials would fall on taxpayers or premiums. On balance the bill helps the people who face care delays more than it costs anyone, but it is a limited fix, not an overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Finance Committee, where no vote or hearing has been scheduled; the bill is still alive only on paper.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced S. 3762, the Prior Authorization Relief Act, in the Senate on February 3, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and the action record shows no further steps since [S4].
One Senate Republican has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: with no committee action and almost no cosponsors, the bill's limits on their approval requirements remain only a proposal.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction; no markup, hearing, or floor consideration appears in the action record.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill with a single Republican cosponsor; no vote has occurred, so no partisan split has been recorded.

industries.note: Standardized prior authorization rules would strip insurers of their most powerful tool for managing costs on high-reimbursement services, the delays and denials that patients experience as barriers to care. Their existing approval requirements are exactly what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Accountable care organizations and other two-sided risk providers
industries.note: The bill exempts their services from the standardized requirements, making risk-bearing arrangements the favored channel for less paperwork. That could pull more care into those models without a guarantee patients see faster care everywhere else.
Fewer and simpler approval requirements on high-cost services would cut administrative staff time and speed payment, alongside the benefit to their patients.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no committee action since referral, and no leadership attention, the bill is likely to sit in the Finance Committee until the 119th Congress ends without a vote, as most Senate bills do.
